_readme: Hand-labelable regression set for the rubric grader (read by tests/grader.test.js and tests/curriculum.spec.js). Drafted by Claude on 2026-09-01 from the theory questions in js/curriculum/lessons.js; PLEASE SPOT-CHECK the labels. label: correct = should pass; partial = names some required ideas but misses or misstates key ones (should not pass, score in the middle band); incorrect = should fail. note = why it was labeled that way. Adversarial samples (added 2026-09-23 for rubric-2) are all incorrect and their note starts with the attack: hint-paste, label-paste, question-copy, learn-paste, keyword-dump, negated or phrase-dump; they were generated from js/curriculum/lessons.js so the pasted text is exact.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Two physical factors (lighting, distance/angle) plus the threshold conclusion.
samples.answer: Ambient lighting is different — the gym has different lights than the workshop so a different amount of light reflects into the sensor. Distance to the element also matters because reflected light falls off with distance squared, and the sensor angle changes how much light bounces back. A fixed threshold like red > 150 fails because the raw number depends on these conditions, not just on the object's color, so the same red element can be above the threshold in one room and below it in another.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Terse paraphrase; still names lighting and distance and explains why one cutoff fails.
samples.answer: The room lighting changed (gym vs workshop) and the sensor is probably a slightly different distance or angle from the element, and light drops off with distance. Since the raw reading changes with the environment, one hardcoded cutoff won't work everywhere — it would detect red in one room and miss it in the other.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Only one factor and the wrong conclusion (just lower the threshold).
samples.answer: The lighting at competition is different so the values come out lower. You should use a lower threshold at competition so it still detects red.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Blames hardware failure, no physical reasoning, keeps a fixed threshold.
samples.answer: The sensor is probably broken or the battery was low. You need to recalibrate the threshold to 100 and it will work again.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Ratio-based explanation, channels scale together, hue stays put.
samples.answer: Hue describes the color as an angle computed from the ratios between the red, green and blue channels rather than their absolute values. When the lighting gets dimmer, all three channels drop together, so the ratios stay roughly the same and the hue barely moves, while the raw RGB numbers all change.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Shorter, still says RGB is absolute and hue is a relationship between channels.
samples.answer: RGB values are absolute brightness numbers so they all scale up or down with the lighting. Hue is based on the relationship between the channels, so if everything gets darker by the same amount the hue stays about the same.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Asserts HSV is better without the ratio/absolute reasoning.
samples.answer: Hue is a different color space that is more accurate for detecting colors, so it works better in different lighting conditions than RGB does.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Invents a hue photodiode; claims immunity to light.
samples.answer: HSV is better because the sensor measures hue directly with a dedicated hue photodiode, so it is not affected by light at all.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Explains outlier dilution and computes (15+14+3)/3 ≈ 10.7.
samples.answer: A single reading of 3 is an outlier — a spike from noise. Reacting to it directly would make the robot think something is suddenly close and do the wrong thing. A moving average blends each reading with its neighbours so one spike is diluted instead of driving a decision. With a window of 3, at the point of the 3 the average is (15 + 14 + 3) / 3 = 32 / 3 ≈ 10.7, which is much closer to the real distance than 3.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Same ideas, less formal; number is right.
samples.answer: If you act on every raw reading, one glitch like the 3 triggers a false reaction. Averaging the last three readings smooths that out: at that point the average is (15+14+3)/3 which is about 10.7 rather than 3, so the spike is mostly filtered out.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Right idea about smoothing, wrong computation.
samples.answer: A moving average smooths the readings so the spike doesn't matter as much and the robot doesn't overreact. The average at that point would be 3 because that's the reading.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Replaces the filter with a hardcoded ignore and gets the average wrong.
samples.answer: You should just ignore any reading below 5 with an if statement. The moving average would show 15 because it ignores the bad value.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Defines both, gives the reliability reason, describes the feedback loop physically.
samples.answer: Open-loop drives the motors for a fixed time or power and hopes the robot ends up in the right place; closed-loop measures where the robot actually is (encoders, odometry, a distance sensor) and keeps correcting the motor output until the error is zero. It is more reliable because battery voltage, friction and wheel slip change the result of the same command. The 'loop' is the flow of information: the motors move the robot, sensors measure the result, that measurement feeds back to the controller, which adjusts the motors again.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Compact; sensor → controller → motor → sensor loop stated.
samples.answer: Open loop = no feedback, just a command. Closed loop = read a sensor, compare to the target, adjust, repeat. Closed loop handles variation like battery level or slipping because it corrects itself. The loop is sensor to controller to motor to robot moving to sensor reading again — the output feeds back into the input.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Says sensors make it more accurate but misidentifies the loop as a while loop.
samples.answer: Closed loop uses sensors so it is more accurate. Open loop doesn't use sensors. The loop means the code runs inside a while loop until it is done.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Backwards conclusion and a misconception about the loop.
samples.answer: Open-loop is better because it is simpler and faster. Closed-loop means the program is stuck in an infinite loop waiting for the sensor, which is why it is unreliable.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Battery voltage and friction/slip, plus no feedback.
samples.answer: Motor power is a percentage of the battery voltage, so as the battery drains the motor spins slower and the robot travels less in the same 2 seconds. Friction and wheel slip also vary — carpet versus tile, dust, or a heavier load change how much the wheels actually move the robot. Nothing is measuring the distance, so the error is never corrected.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Names battery, wheel slip, friction, motor temperature.
samples.answer: Battery voltage drops during a match so 0.5 power isn't the same speed every time, and things like wheel slip, floor friction and motor temperature change how far you go. Time-based driving has no feedback to fix that.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Only one factor.
samples.answer: The battery gets lower over time so the robot goes slower and doesn't travel as far.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Denies the premise.
samples.answer: It does travel the same distance because 0.5 power is always the same speed; any difference comes from the driver pressing start at a slightly different time.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Stiff spring → overshoot → pulled back → oscillation.
samples.answer: kP acts like a spring pulling the robot toward the target — the farther away, the harder it pulls. If kP is too high the spring is too stiff: the robot accelerates hard, overshoots the target because it can't stop instantly, then the spring yanks it back the other way and it overshoots again. That back-and-forth is oscillation, and without enough damping it can grow instead of settling.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Momentum carries past, bounces around the setpoint.
samples.answer: With a very stiff spring the robot gets pulled toward the setpoint so hard that its momentum carries it past, then it gets pulled back past it again. It keeps bouncing around the target instead of settling — that's oscillation.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Describes jerkiness but not the overshoot/oscillation mechanism or the spring.
samples.answer: If kP is too high the robot moves too fast and is jerky, so you should lower it until it moves smoothly.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Inverts the analogy.
samples.answer: A high kP makes the spring too loose, so the robot never reaches the target and stops short of it.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Track width divides the wheel difference; heading under-reported; position integrates along wrong heading.
samples.answer: Heading is calculated from the difference between the left and right wheel distances divided by the track width. If the track width constant is too large, every difference gets divided by a bigger number, so the computed heading changes less than the real heading did — the reported heading slowly drifts away from the true heading. Then, even driving perfectly straight, each position update is added along the wrong heading, so the x and y estimate curves away from the true path and the error accumulates the farther you go.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Same mechanism, shorter.
samples.answer: Track width is the divisor when converting the left/right wheel difference into rotation. Too wide means the code under-reports turning, so the heading estimate drifts. Since each little step of x and y is added in the direction of the estimated heading, a wrong heading makes the position drift sideways over time even on a straight line.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: States the outcome without the mechanism.
samples.answer: The heading will be wrong and the robot will think it is turning a little. Because of that the position will be off too.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Claims heading is unaffected.
samples.answer: A wider track width doesn't affect heading, it only makes the robot think it drove farther, so x is too big but the heading stays correct.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Start, arcs toward but not through the control point, ends; obstacle/smoothness reason.
samples.answer: It starts at (24, 24), arcs upward toward the control point at (72, 96) without actually touching it, and ends at (120, 24), so it's a smooth symmetric hump because the control point is centered between the endpoints. You'd choose it to go around something on the field, like an obstacle or game element, or to approach the end from a better angle, while keeping the motion smooth instead of stop-and-turn.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Compact; bows in +y, doesn't reach the control point, obstacle avoidance.
samples.answer: A single arc: it begins at (24,24), bows up in the positive y direction toward (72,96) but doesn't reach it, then comes back down to (120,24). Use it when a straight line would hit an obstacle or when you want a smooth continuous path rather than sharp corners.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Thinks the curve passes through the control point; no reason for choosing it.
samples.answer: It makes a curve from the start to the end that goes through the control point at (72, 96).

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Describes two straight lines with a corner.
samples.answer: The curve goes straight from (24,24) to (72,96) and then straight to (120,24) — two lines with a corner at the control point.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Steady-state error; add I (impatience) and/or anti-gravity feedforward; warns about kP.
samples.answer: That's steady-state error: the proportional term is too small to overcome gravity and friction once the error is tiny — the spring is too weak at 8 degrees to lift the heavy arm. Add the integral term (the impatience term), which accumulates the leftover error over time and keeps pushing until it's gone, or add a feedforward anti-gravity term that supplies the constant power needed to hold the arm against gravity. Increasing kP a bit could help but risks oscillation.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Same answer, informal.
samples.answer: The arm stops short because at a small error P alone doesn't produce enough power to fight gravity — steady-state error. Add kI (impatience — it builds up while the error persists) or an anti-gravity feedforward so there's a constant holding force. Don't just crank kP or you'll get oscillation.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Only suggests raising kP; no integral/feedforward, no risk noted.
samples.answer: Increase kP so it pushes harder and reaches the target.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Misuses the damper term.
samples.answer: Add more kD, the damper, because damping will push the arm the rest of the way to the target.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Three genuinely different layers (hardware, configuration, input) each with a no-code test.
samples.answer: 1) Hardware or wiring: the motor cable or port is bad — test by swapping the motor to a known-good port or running it from the Robot Controller's configuration test screen. 2) Configuration: the motor name in the config doesn't match the code — check the configuration on the Driver Hub and compare the name. 3) Input: the gamepad isn't registered as gamepad 1 or the A press isn't reaching the code — press Start+A to bind the gamepad and watch the gamepad indicator on the Driver Hub. Each test isolates one cause without touching the code.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Compact version of the same three hypotheses and tests.
samples.answer: Could be the motor or wiring (test: run it from the config screen), the config name not matching (test: read the Driver Hub config against the code), or the gamepad not paired (test: press Start+A and check the gamepad icon). Those are different layers: hardware, configuration, input.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Three variations of one idea (wiring), one test.
samples.answer: Maybe the motor is unplugged, maybe the wire is loose, or maybe the port is broken. Check the cable and plug it back in.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Changes code, one hypothesis.
samples.answer: The code has a bug, so add a print statement and change the button to B to see if it works.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Intermittent/timing category, logging-and-compare approach.
samples.answer: That's an intermittent, timing-related bug — it depends on something that varies between runs like timing, sensor noise, loop speed or battery, not on logic that is wrong every time. The approach is to add logging and telemetry that record state transitions and sensor values every loop so you can capture what was different on the failing runs, look for a race between the follower being busy and the state machine advancing, and check any timeout or isBusy() condition that can flicker.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Short; intermittent, log everything, compare good vs bad runs.
samples.answer: It's an intermittent timing bug. Since it isn't reproducible every time, log everything — state, sensor readings, loop time — and compare a good run with a bad run to find the difference, instead of guessing.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Wrong category (deterministic logic), generic approach.
samples.answer: It's a logic bug in the state machine. Read through the code carefully to find the mistake and fix it.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Nonsense category.
samples.answer: It's a compile error that only happens sometimes; rebuild the code and it will go away.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Masks the cause, hurts loop timing, names concrete root causes and a telemetry investigation.
samples.answer: The sleep just masks the problem: it doesn't explain why the motor sometimes ignores the press, it only changes the timing so the failure is less visible, and it makes the whole loop slower so every other control feels laggy. The real cause is probably something like another piece of code overwriting the motor power later in the same loop, the loop being so slow that short presses are missed, or a state machine that resets. Investigate by adding telemetry for the button state and the motor power each loop to see what actually happens on a missed press.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Symptom vs cause stated, loop stall, override/timing/config candidates.
samples.answer: Adding sleep treats the symptom — the intake still fails for the same reason, it's just hidden, and now the loop stalls for 200 ms which hurts driving. Look for what's overriding the motor power (two places setting it), whether the button read is being missed because of loop timing, or a wiring or config issue, using telemetry to watch the values.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Notices the slowdown but no root-cause reasoning or investigation.
samples.answer: Sleep makes the code slow so you should remove it and try again.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Defends the sleep as the fix.
samples.answer: It is a root cause fix because the motor needs time to respond; the real problem is that 200 ms is not enough, so use 500 ms.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Ordered checks (OpMode/init, config/hub, code-side block via telemetry) and a park-only fallback.
samples.answer: First, check the obvious physical things: is the right OpMode selected, did the robot actually finish init (telemetry shows it), is battery voltage okay. Second, check configuration: was the robot configuration changed or the wrong config active, and does the Driver Hub show any warning. Third, check for a code-side block: something after waitForStart like a sensor init, a path build crash, or a timer that started before Start — look at telemetry to see where it's stuck. Fallback: switch to the simpler backup autonomous (drive forward and park) that's already loaded so you still score the park points, and fix the real one between matches.

samples.label: correct
samples.note: Numbered steps, same order, backup auto.
samples.answer: 1) Right OpMode selected and init actually completed? 2) Config file and hub status — any errors, correct robot config? 3) Read telemetry for where it's stuck after Start (sensor, path build, exception). If nothing works in 4 minutes, run the basic park-only backup auto and debug later.

samples.label: partial
samples.note: Restart only, no diagnostic order, no fallback plan.
samples.answer: Restart the robot and try again. If it still doesn't work, restart it again and hope it works in the match.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: Unrealistic and not a diagnostic process.
samples.answer: Rewrite the autonomous from scratch in the 4 minutes — there's enough time if you type fast.

Reflected light drops with distance (roughly distance squared) and depends on the sensor angle and the surface. samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: learn-paste: the lesson text (HTML stripped) pasted back as the answer.
samples.answer: Every sensor reading = signal (real value) + noise (random variation). Sources of noise in FTC: electronic noise (ADC precision limits cause ±1-3 count fluctuation), mechanical vibration (robot shakes while driving, sensor moves relative to surface), electromagnetic interference (spinning motors generate fields that induce currents in sensor wires). A distance reading of 15.2cm means the wall is probably between 14.5-15.9cm. Next cycle it might read 14.8 or 15.5 even though nothing moved. Reacting to one reading is dangerous — one noisy spike of 8cm triggers your state transition when the wall is actually 14cm away. Filtering combats noise: threshold counting (require N consecutive readings), moving average (average last 5 readings), or exponential smoothing ( filtered = α × new + (1-α) × previous ).

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: learn-paste: the lesson text (HTML stripped) pasted back as the answer.
samples.answer: Imagine throwing a basketball at a hoop with your eyes closed . You line up, throw with a specific force, and hope. That’s open-loop control — executing a pre-planned action without checking the result. In FTC, open-loop looks like setPower(0.5); sleep(2000); — run at 50% for 2 seconds and hope it’s the right distance. It fails because: Battery voltage drops during a match (13.5V → 12.0V), so the same power command produces different speeds. Friction varies across the field — dusty tiles vs clean tiles. Weight changes when you pick up game elements, shifting the center of gravity. Open-loop assumes a perfectly predictable world. The world is not predictable.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: learn-paste: the lesson text (HTML stripped) pasted back as the answer.
samples.answer: P = A Spring. Attach a spring between your robot and the target. Far away → strong pull. Close → gentle pull. force = kP × error . High kP = stiff spring (aggressive correction, might overshoot and oscillate). Low kP = loose spring (slow approach, might never arrive). D = A Shock Absorber. A spring alone oscillates — that’s why cars have shock absorbers. D resists motion proportional to speed of approach. braking = kD × speed_of_approach . It prevents the robot from blowing past the target. I = Impatience. Sometimes P gets you close but friction prevents the last bit of movement. I accumulates error over time, building up extra force until it pushes past friction. Danger: too much accumulation = integral windup = massive overshoot once the robot finally moves. F = Anti-Gravity. If an arm needs 0.15 power just to hold position against gravity, kF provides that baseline so PID only handles corrections. Remove the constant load so the fine-tuning system can focus.

samples.label: incorrect
samples.note: learn-paste: the lesson text (HTML stripped) pasted back as the answer.
samples.answer: Not all bugs are the same. The category tells you where to look: Configuration bugs — code is correct but references wrong things. Hardware Map mismatches, wrong motor direction. Cause immediate crashes or obvious wrong behavior. Easiest to find. Logic bugs — code doesn’t crash but does the wrong thing. Wrong state transitions, bad PID constants, wrong comparisons. No error message — code does exactly what you told it, which isn’t what you wanted. Timing bugs — works sometimes, not always. Race conditions, wrong ordering, sensors checked before stabilizing. Hardest because they’re intermittent. Integration bugs — two pieces work alone but break together. Two controllers fighting over one motor, double update() calls. Only appear when the full system is assembled.
